---
title: "4.1 The Derivative: A Ratio at One Moment"
---

## The problem

A chemist follows the disappearance of a reactant A and fits the concentration to
$$[\mathrm{A}](t) = 0.80\,e^{-0.139\,t} \qquad ([\mathrm{A}] \text{ in M},\; t \text{ in minutes}).$$
Her kinetics textbook says that the rate at which A disappears is proportional to
how much A is present *right now*. Notice the phrase. A rate law is a statement
about a single instant: it ties the speed at this moment to the concentration at this
moment. But every rate we have computed so far was a rate over an *interval* —
"0.60 M lost in ten minutes," or the slope of a calibration line between two
standards. How does one extract a speed at *one moment* from a function that only
gives concentrations at moments?

The question has the shape of a trap, and it is worth seeing the trap clearly before
escaping it. A speed is a change divided by an elapsed time. At a single instant, no
time elapses and nothing changes: the ratio is zero divided by zero. The rest of this
section is the story of how that meaningless ratio becomes the most useful quantity
in physical chemistry.

## What an average rate is, and what is wrong with it

Pick any two times, $t$ and $t+h$. The *average rate* of change of $[\mathrm{A}]$ over
that interval is
$$\frac{[\mathrm{A}](t+h)-[\mathrm{A}](t)}{h} \qquad (\text{units: M/min}).$$
Geometrically it is the slope of the *secant line* through the two points on the
graph. This is a perfectly good physical quantity — but ask it for the rate at
$t = 0$ and it gives an unsettling answer. Starting at $t=0$ and looking forward
five minutes gives $-0.080$ M/min; looking forward one minute gives $-0.104$ M/min;
looking forward a tenth of a minute gives $-0.110$ M/min. Three different answers for
the *same moment*.

The reason is that each answer quietly contains a choice you made: the length $h$ of
the interval. An average rate is a property of the interval you picked, not of the
chemistry at the moment you care about. What we want is the average rate with that
arbitrary choice removed.

## Shrinking the interval: the ratio settles

If the choice of $h$ is the problem, let it shrink and watch what the quotient does.
The table follows $[\mathrm{A}](t) = 0.80\,e^{-0.139t}$ from $t = 0$.

| $h$ (min) | change in $[\mathrm{A}]$ (M) | quotient $\Delta[\mathrm{A}]/h$ (M/min) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 5 | $-0.40074$ | $-0.08015$ |
| 1 | $-0.10382$ | $-0.10382$ |
| 0.1 | $-0.01104$ | $-0.11043$ |
| 0.01 | $-0.00111$ | $-0.11112$ |
| 0.001 | $-0.00011$ | $-0.11119$ |

Look at the middle column and then at the last one, because the whole idea lives in
the contrast between them. The change in concentration is collapsing toward zero —
by a factor of ten each row — and so is the elapsed time $h$. Both parts of the ratio
are vanishing. Yet the *ratio* does not vanish; it creeps toward a definite number,
$-0.1112$ M/min. **A ratio of two vanishing quantities need not vanish. When
numerator and denominator shrink together in step, the ratio can settle.** That
settled value — which no single interval produces but which every short enough interval
approximates — is what "the rate at an instant" has to mean.

::: {.env .remark}
Press play in the [derivative studio](derivative-studio.html) and watch both
quantities collapse while the quotient locks onto its limit. Then move the anchor
time $t_0$: the limit changes with the moment you ask about, so the instantaneous
rate is itself a *function* of time.
:::

## Making it a definition

The table suggests a definition, and the symbols are worth reading in words.

::: {.env .definition}
**Definition 4.1.1 (derivative).** For a function $f$ and a point $x$, the
*derivative* of $f$ at $x$ is the number the difference quotient settles to as the
interval shrinks:
$$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\; \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h},$$
whenever that limit exists. In Leibniz's notation the same number is written
$\dfrac{df}{dx}$.
:::

Three readings of $\dfrac{df}{dx}$ are useful and should be held together. It is the
**instantaneous rate**: how fast $f$ is changing per unit $x$ at this moment. It is
the **slope of the tangent line**: the secant line pivots toward the tangent as
$h \to 0$. And it is the **best straight-line approximation**: near $x$, the function
behaves like the line through $(x, f(x))$ with slope $f'(x)$ — the very reason that
the shortcut $e^{x} \approx 1 + x$ you used on the exam works near zero.
Notice too what the symbol is *not*: $\frac{df}{dx}$ is not a fraction of two tiny
numbers to be cancelled. It is the name of the settled value of a ratio, and its
units are always (units of output) per (unit of input) — here M/min.

## Why you cannot just set $h = 0$ — and what actually happens

If the quotient is $0/0$ at $h = 0$, how can its value at $h$ near zero be
meaningful? Because the algebra can often remove the problem *before* $h$ goes to
zero. The common factor that makes the numerator vanish is also in the denominator;
cancel it while $h \neq 0$, and what is left has no difficulty at $h = 0$.

Take the simplest nontrivial function, $f(t) = t^{2}$:
$$\frac{(t+h)^{2} - t^{2}}{h} = \frac{2th + h^{2}}{h} = 2t + h \;\longrightarrow\; 2t \quad (h \to 0).$$
The numerator is not merely small: it is $h$ times something ($2t + h$). That
structure — *numerator proportional to $h$* — is exactly what lets the ratio survive
the collapse.

::: {.env .example}
**Example 4.1.1 — a filling reactor, from the definition.** The product amount in a
batch reactor is $n(t) = 3.0\,t - 0.25\,t^{2}$ (mol, $t$ in hours). Find $n'(t)$ and
then the rate at $t = 2$ h.

*Setting it up.* The derivative is the settled value of
$[\,n(t+h) - n(t)\,]/h$. Everything hinges on expanding $n(t+h)$ and spotting the
common factor.

*Solution.*
$$n(t+h) - n(t) = 3.0h - 0.25\,(2th + h^{2}) = h\,(3.0 - 0.50\,t - 0.25\,h).$$
Dividing by $h$:
$$\frac{n(t+h)-n(t)}{h} = 3.0 - 0.50\,t - 0.25\,h \;\longrightarrow\; n'(t) = 3.0 - 0.50\,t \quad (h \to 0).$$
At $t = 2$ h: $n'(2) = 2.0$ mol/h.

*Check.* At $t = 2$ the quotient is $2.0 - 0.25\,h$, so the numerical values for
$h = 2,\, 1,\, 0.5,\, 0.1$ are $1.50,\, 1.75,\, 1.875,\, 1.975$ mol/h, creeping to $2.0$
exactly as the formula says. Units: mol per hour. Limiting case: at $t = 0$ the rate
is $3.0$ mol/h, the *initial* rate, and it falls linearly as the reactor depletes
its reagent — the sign and trend a filling-then-saturating process should have.
:::

## The exponential: where first-order kinetics comes from

Now return to the chemist's function. Writing $[\mathrm{A}](t+h) = 0.80\,e^{-0.139t}\,e^{-0.139h}$,
the quotient becomes
$$\frac{[\mathrm{A}](t+h)-[\mathrm{A}](t)}{h} = 0.80\,e^{-0.139\,t}\cdot\frac{e^{-0.139\,h} - 1}{h} = [\mathrm{A}](t)\cdot\frac{e^{-0.139\,h} - 1}{h}.$$
Something remarkable has happened: the whole dependence on the moment $t$ has factored
out as $[\mathrm{A}](t)$, and all the $h$-dependence sits in one clean factor. That
factor settles as $h$ shrinks:

| $h$ | 1 | 0.1 | 0.01 | 0.001 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $\dfrac{e^{-0.139h}-1}{h}$ | $-0.12977$ | $-0.13804$ | $-0.13890$ | $-0.13899$ |

— toward $-0.139$. Therefore
$$\frac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = -0.139\,[\mathrm{A}](t).$$
This is the chemical payoff of the section. The statement "the rate of disappearance
is proportional to the amount present" is not an extra physical assumption stacked on
top of the exponential: it is what the exponential *is*, read through the definition
of the derivative. Conversely, a first-order rate law $-d[\mathrm{A}]/dt = k[\mathrm{A}]$
forces the concentration to decay exponentially. At $t = 0$ the rate is
$-0.139 \times 0.80 = -0.1112$ M/min — the number the table was approaching — and at
$t = 10$ min, with $0.199$ M left, it has fallen to $-0.0277$ M/min. The *same* curve
has a different slope at every moment, which is why the derivative is itself a
function.

## Remarks and cautions

::: {.env .caution}
**An average rate is not an instantaneous rate.** Reporting $-0.080$ M/min as "the
rate at $t=0$" because you measured over five minutes is the secant-for-tangent
error. The two agree only when the curve is straight (a zero-order reaction), and the
gap between them is exactly what shrinking $h$ closes.
:::

::: {.env .caution}
**Units come with the derivative.** $d[\mathrm{A}]/dt$ is in M/min, not M. A derivative
reported without its "per-input" unit is incomplete — and, as the next section will
show, a missing unit is the quickest way to catch a dropped factor.
:::

::: {.env .remark}
The limit must come out the same whether $h$ shrinks through positive values
(looking forward) or negative values (looking back). At a sharp corner — the kink in
a heating curve at a phase boundary, say — the two disagree and no derivative exists
there. Smooth chemical functions do not have this problem.
:::

## Summary

A rate over an interval is a ratio, and the interval length is an arbitrary choice
that contaminates the answer; the rate at an instant is that same ratio with the
choice removed. Shrinking the interval makes numerator and denominator both vanish,
yet the ratio settles to a definite number whenever the numerator is proportional to
$h$ — the algebraic fact that lets us cancel $h$ before letting it go to zero. That
settled value is the derivative, readable three ways: as an instantaneous rate, as a
tangent slope, and as the best straight-line approximation, with units of output per
input. For the exponential decay $[\mathrm{A}] = 0.80\,e^{-0.139t}$ the whole moment
dependence factors out and the derivative is $-0.139\,[\mathrm{A}]$ — first-order
kinetics, derived rather than assumed. What the limit definition does *not* give us
is speed: each function required its own expansion and its own cancellation. The next
section asks whether chemistry's functions are built from a few pieces whose
derivatives we can establish once and reuse forever.
